questions.question: Which event creates a new Spark stage boundary?
options: A projection that keeps two columns from one input partition
A filter that removes rows inside each existing partition
A shuffle that regroups records from many parent partitions by key
A local expression that converts one timestamp to a date
questions.explanation: A wide dependency requires data from several parent partitions, so Spark materializes an exchange and schedules the downstream work as a new stage.

questions.question: A shuffle writes 600 GiB and the initial target is 256 MiB per partition. What is the starting partition estimate?
options: About 240 partitions
About 600 partitions
About 1,200 partitions
About 2,400 partitions
questions.explanation: 600 GiB is 614,400 MiB. Dividing by 256 MiB gives 2,400 partitions before adjusting for skew, scheduler overhead, slots, and measured task memory.

questions.question: One customer owns 40% of rows for a group-by key. Why can adding executors leave the stage slow?
options: The same hot key still maps to one reducer partition unless the key distribution changes
Executors disable Spark's optimizer when a key is skewed
Every executor must process every partition in a group-by
Additional executors force the driver to collect all rows
questions.explanation: More slots cannot subdivide a single hot reducer partition. Salting, skew-aware processing, pre-aggregation, or isolating the dominant key changes the work distribution.

questions.question: When is a broadcast join defensible?
options: Whenever the larger table has more partitions than the cluster has cores
When the projected small side is measured, bounded below a reviewed safety limit, and can fit on every executor
Whenever the source data is compressed on disk
Only when both sides of the join have exactly the same partition count
questions.explanation: Broadcasting copies the small side to executor processes. Its projected in-memory size and cluster-wide network and memory cost must be bounded and measured.

questions.question: What trade-off usually comes with very large executors?
options: They prevent all shuffle fetch failures
They make every transformation a narrow dependency
One process failure removes more task slots, cached blocks, and local shuffle output
They guarantee that no task spills to disk
questions.explanation: More cores and state share one process fate. Large executors reduce some process overhead but increase failure blast radius and concurrent pressure on one heap.

questions.question: Why must a task that writes to an external service be idempotent?
options: Spark may retry or speculatively run a task attempt more than once
Idempotency lets the driver avoid building a physical plan
External services always return rows in partition order
Idempotency removes the need for timeouts
questions.explanation: A failed or slow task can have another attempt. Without a stable operation identity or transactional boundary, repeated attempts can duplicate a business effect.

questions.question: What does a Structured Streaming watermark primarily control?
options: The number of executor cores assigned to each trigger
How long event-time state remains eligible for late data before it can be retired
Whether the source supports replay after driver failure
The compression codec used for checkpoint files
questions.explanation: A watermark bounds event-time state and late-data acceptance. It trades state and recovery cost against how much lateness the query will incorporate.

questions.question: Which evidence best identifies a skew-driven stage bottleneck?
options: Average cluster CPU alone
The driver's source-code line count
Median task duration without partition bytes
Maximum task input and duration far above the median, concentrated in a few partitions
questions.explanation: Skew appears in the distribution of partition bytes, rows, spill, and task duration. Averages can look healthy while one straggling partition controls stage completion.
